# 17-Week Plan: 25 m to 200 m Continuous by 20 March

You have about **17 weeks**, or roughly 33 pool sessions. That's a realistic timeline. Going from 25 m to 200 m is mostly a matter of **breathing rhythm and pacing**, not fitness, and both improve quickly with regular practice.

## Before you start
- **See your GP** for a quick check, especially if you have heart, blood pressure or breathing concerns. Mention that you'll be swimming in the sea.
- **Consider a few lessons** if the pool offers adult coaching. One or two sessions on breathing technique can save you weeks.
- **Bring a water bottle** to every session. You dehydrate in the pool more than you'd think.

## The key skill: breathing
Most people who stop at 25 m are holding their breath, not running out of fitness. Aim for this rhythm:
- **Pull** with your arms and lift your face to breathe in.
- **Kick and glide** with your face down, blowing out slowly through your nose and mouth.
- **Exhale fully underwater** every stroke, so you're only breathing *in* when you lift.

Swim **slower than feels necessary**. Slow and relaxed beats fast and puffed.

## Session format (30–45 min)
1. **Warm-up:** 5 min walking or gentle swimming in the shallow end
2. **Main set:** see the weekly plan below
3. **Cool-down:** 3–5 min easy floating or slow swimming

"Rest" means standing at the wall and catching your breath. "Continuous" means turning at the wall without holding on or standing.

## Week-by-week plan

**Phase 1: Breathing and comfort (Weeks 1–4)**

**Phase 4: 200 m and sea preparation (Weeks 14–17)**

| 15 | 2 Mar | 1 × 200 m, rest 3 min, plus 2 × 50 m. Practise stopping mid-pool: tread water or float on your back for 30 sec, then carry on. |
| 16 | 9 Mar | 1 × 200 m, then 1 × 100 m. Add 50 m extra if it feels easy, because sea swimming feels harder than pool swimming. |
| 17 | 16 Mar | Tuesday only: an easy 200 m to boost confidence. Then pack! |

## Rules for progressing
- **Move on** only when the current week feels manageable. Repeating a week is completely normal.
- **There is a buffer built in.** If you reach 200 m by week 14, you have three weeks to consolidate. If you're behind, weeks 15–16 give you room to catch up.
- **Back off** if anything aches, particularly your knees (the breaststroke kick can strain them), shoulders or neck. Rest a session rather than push through.
- **Keep active on other days.** Brisk walks of 20–30 minutes on non-pool days build stamina and cost you nothing.

## Swimming in the sea at Okinawa
The sea is different from a pool, so plan for it:
- **The water will be cool.** In March it's typically around 21–22 °C. Consider a **shorty wetsuit or swim top**, which also adds buoyancy. Get in slowly to let your breathing settle.
- **There are no walls to hold.** That's why weeks 15–16 include floating and treading water. Rolling onto your back to rest is your safety valve.
- **Swim parallel to the shore** in shallow water rather than straight out into deep water. You can be out and back with your granddaughter while staying within standing depth.
- **Never swim alone.** Have a strong swimmer nearby and check for lifeguards, currents and jellyfish warnings on the day.
- **Consider a tow float.** It's a bright inflatable buoy clipped to your waist that you can hold if you need a break. It's cheap, makes you visible, and is popular with open-water swimmers of all ages.
- **The distance doesn't need to be 200 m.** If the conditions are choppy, a short swim together will be just as memorable.

You've already got the hardest part sorted, which is the motivation. Twice a week, steady progress, and you'll be well prepared for a very special swim. Congratulations to your granddaughter! 🌊

# Your 200-Metre Plan: 20 November to 20 March

You have **17 weeks** and about **33 pool sessions**. Going from 25 m to 200 m in that time is realistic. Most people who stop at 25 m are short of breath, not short of fitness, so the early weeks focus on breathing and gliding. Distance comes after that.

## Before you start

- **See your GP** before the first session. At 67, it's sensible to have your heart and blood pressure checked before a new training programme.
- **Buy goggles** if you don't already have a pair. Putting your face in the water is the biggest single energy-saver in breaststroke.
- **Holiday closures:** Christmas Day and New Year's Day both fall on Fridays this year, so the pool will probably be shut. The plan allows for this.
- **Rule for every session:** "Rest" means standing or holding the wall until your breathing settles. If you get chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, stop and get out.

## The three habits that get you past 25 m

1. **Breathe out underwater.** Let a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth while your face is in the water. Then lift, take a breath in, and put your face back down. Holding your breath is what makes you stop at 25 m.
2. **Glide.** After each kick, stay stretched out with your arms forward for a slow count of "one-two." Pull, breathe, kick, glide. Slower strokes use less energy.
3. **Swim at an easy pace.** You should be able to swim at a pace you could keep up all morning. Gasping means you're going too fast.

**Each session:** 5 minutes of easy warm-up (walking in the water, a couple of gentle widths), then the main set below, then 5 minutes of easy floating or walking to cool down. Allow 40–45 minutes in total.

## Week-by-week plan

Distances assume a 25 m pool. Until Week 15, touching the wall and pushing straight off counts as "not stopping."

| Week | Sessions | Main set | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Fri 20 Nov | 6 × 25 m, 60 s rest | Practise breathing out underwater: 10 bubble-breaths holding the wall before you start |
| **2** | Tue 24, Fri 27 Nov | 8 × 25 m, 45 s rest | Learn to float on your back for 30 s. This is your safety skill for the sea |
| **3** | Tue 1, Fri 4 Dec | 8 × 25 m, 30 s rest. **Fri: 1 × 50 m** | Count "pull, breathe, kick, glide" every stroke |
| **4** | Tue 8, Fri 11 Dec | 3 × 50 m (60 s rest), then 4 × 25 m | Turn at the wall calmly; take one breath and push off |
| **5** | Tue 15, Fri 18 Dec | 4 × 50 m, 45 s rest. **Fri: try 75 m** | Longer glide, fewer strokes per length |
| **6** | Tue 22 Dec (Fri is Christmas) | 2 × 75 m, 2 × 50 m | Keep the habit going over the holidays |
| **7** | Tue 29 Dec (Fri is New Year) | 3 × 75 m, 60 s rest | Same again. Aim for it to feel easier |
| **8** | Tue 5, Fri 8 Jan | 3 × 75 m, 45 s rest | Check that your knees feel fine. Narrow the kick if they ache |
| **9** | Tue 12, Fri 15 Jan | **1 × 100 m**, then 3 × 50 m | First milestone: 100 m |
| **10** | Tue 19, Fri 22 Jan | 2 × 100 m, 90 s rest | Steady, even pace on both swims |
| **11** | Tue 26, Fri 29 Jan | 1 × 125 m, 1 × 100 m | Relax your shoulders and neck when you breathe |
| **12** | Tue 2, Fri 5 Feb | **1 × 150 m**, then 2 × 50 m | Second milestone: 150 m |
| **13** | Tue 9, Fri 12 Feb | 150 m + 100 m, 2 min rest | Build confidence at this distance |
| **14** | Tue 16, Fri 19 Feb | Tue: 175 m. **Fri: 200 m** | Target reached. Celebrate |
| **15** | Tue 23, Fri 26 Feb | 200 m, **without touching the walls** | Stop about 1 m short of each wall and turn around while still swimming, as you would in the sea |
| **16** | Tue 2, Fri 5 Mar | Tue: 200 m no-touch. **Fri: 250 m** | Builds a safety margin, because the sea is harder than the pool |
| **17** | Tue 9, Fri 12 Mar | 200 m no-touch, then 4 × 25 m easy | Keep it relaxed. You're ready |
| **18** | Tue 16 Mar (if before you fly) | Easy 150 m | Light swim only. Save your energy for the trip |

**If a week goes badly** because of a cold, a missed session or a tired day, repeat that week rather than skipping ahead. The plan finishes about four weeks early, so you can lose up to three weeks and still arrive with 200 m in hand.

**Between pool days:** a brisk 30-minute walk on two or three other days a week builds stamina without straining your shoulders.

## In Okinawa: the sea is different from the pool

- **Swimming out and back doubles the distance.** If you swim 100 m out, you need another 100 m to get back. Your 200 m means about 100 m out at most. Choose a turning point before you set off.
- **The water will be cooler.** The sea there in March is typically around 21–22 °C, colder than a heated pool. Cold water can make you gasp on entry, so walk in slowly and splash your face and neck first. A long-sleeved swim top or shorty wetsuit will help, and it also adds buoyancy.
- **Salt water helps you.** You'll float more easily than in the pool.
- **Have a practice swim a day or two before the wedding.** Swim 50–100 m parallel to the shore in water where you can stand, so you get used to the waves and the sea floor.
- **On the day:** stay where you can stand, or have a confident swimmer next to you. If you get tired, roll onto your back and float. That's what Week 2 was for.

You're going from 25 m to 200 m in about 13 weeks with four weeks of spare time. Enjoy the swim with your granddaughter. It will be a wonderful moment for both of you.

# Grade 4 Lesson Plan: The Water Cycle

**Duration:** 50 minutes
**Class size:** 42 pupils, in 7 groups of 6
**Resources:** Blackboard and chalk, plus these items from home:
- a flask of very hot water
- a clear glass jar
- a metal plate or lid
- a few ice cubes in a small container
- 28 paper cards (7 sets of 4)

## Learning Objectives
By the end of the lesson, pupils will be able to:
1. Name the four stages of the water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.
2. Explain what happens to water at each stage.
3. Put the stages in the correct order.

## Before the Lesson
- Write one word on each card: **EVAPORATION**, **CONDENSATION**, **PRECIPITATION**, **COLLECTION**. Make 7 sets and shuffle each set.
- Draw a large water cycle diagram on the blackboard: sun, sea, cloud, rain and a mountain with a river. Leave the four labels blank.

## Lesson Procedure

**1. Introduction (5 minutes)**
Ask: *"Where does rain come from? Where does a puddle go after the sun comes out?"* Take 4–5 answers. Tell pupils that the same water moves around and around, and this is called the water cycle.

**2. Demonstration (10 minutes)**
Gather pupils so all 42 can see. Have the front rows sit and the back rows stand.
- Pour hot water into the glass jar. Point out the steam rising. Write **Evaporation**: the sun heats water and it rises as vapour.
- Put the metal plate on the jar and place ice cubes on top.
- After 2–3 minutes, lift the plate and show the droplets underneath. Write **Condensation**: vapour cools and turns into tiny drops, which form clouds.
- Show the drops falling back into the jar. Write **Precipitation**: drops get heavy and fall as rain, hail or snow.
- Point to the water in the jar. Write **Collection**: water gathers in seas, rivers, lakes and the ground, and the cycle starts again.

**3. Teaching with the Blackboard Diagram (10 minutes)**
Call four pupils to write the four labels in the correct places on the diagram. Draw arrows to show the circle. The class repeats the sequence aloud together: *"Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection."*

**4. Group Activity: "Order the Cycle" (12 minutes)**
- Give each of the 7 groups one shuffled set of 4 cards.
- **Task 1 (5 minutes):** The group arranges the cards in the correct order in a circle on the desk.
- **Task 2 (7 minutes):** Each group picks one stage and prepares a single sentence about it from everyday life. Example: *"When mother hangs wet clothes in the sun, the water evaporates."*
- The teacher walks around and checks each group's order. Two groups share their sentence with the class.

**5. Quiz (10 minutes)**
Pupils copy the questions from the board and answer in their exercise books.

1. What is it called when the sun heats water and it turns into vapour?
2. What is it called when water vapour cools and forms clouds?
3. Name two kinds of precipitation.
4. Name two places where water collects.
5. Write the four stages of the water cycle in the correct order.

**Answers:**
1. Evaporation
2. Condensation
3. Any two of: rain, hail, snow
4. Any two of: sea, river, lake, pond, the ground
5. Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection

**6. Conclusion (3 minutes)**
Pupils exchange books with a neighbour and mark them as you read the answers aloud. End by asking: *"Will the rain that falls today ever come back to the sky?"* The answer is yes, because the cycle never stops.

# Your 8-Week Moving Plan: Lyon → Porto (15 January)

You have exactly 8 weeks, with Christmas and New Year in the middle. The plan front-loads the big decisions so the holiday weeks can stay light. **Nothing on this list requires you to lift anything heavy.** Where lifting is involved, someone else does it.

---

## Week 1 (18–22 Nov): Decide and book
- [ ] **Measure the Porto flat** (or ask the landlord or agent for a floor plan). Note room sizes, door widths, and whether there's a lift.
- [ ] **Choose what comes with you.** Walk through the house with coloured stickers: green = Porto, yellow = maybe, red = goes.
- [ ] **Call the movers back with these questions:**
  - How many m³ is half a truck? A 52 m² flat usually needs about 15–20 m³, so half a truck is likely enough.
  - Does the price include **packing, dismantling, and reassembly**? (Given your back, ask for packing to be included even if it costs more.)
  - Is **insurance** included, and up to what value?
  - Porto has narrow streets. Can the truck reach your building, or will they need a smaller shuttle van? Is that in the price?
  - What are the exact pickup and delivery dates?
- [ ] **Get one more quote** to compare, then **book before the end of November.** Companies fill up around the holidays.

## Week 2 (23–29 Nov): Paperwork in France
- [ ] **Health cover:** If you receive a French pension, ask your pension fund (CNAV/CARSAT) or CPAM for an **S1 form**. It keeps your French-funded healthcare valid in Portugal.
- [ ] **Taxes:** Update your address on impots.gouv.fr once you have a move date, and ask how your pension will be taxed after you leave.
- [ ] Book an appointment with your **doctor** for a check-up, repeat prescriptions (enough for 2–3 months), and copies of your medical records.
- [ ] Tell your **bank** you're moving abroad. Check its fees for using your card in Portugal.

## Week 3 (30 Nov–6 Dec): Start clearing furniture
- [ ] List furniture to sell on **Leboncoin** (buyers collect it themselves, so ask them to bring help).
- [ ] Book a free collection from **Emmaüs** or a local charity for what doesn't sell. Book early, because December slots go fast.
- [ ] Offer anything sentimental to family and friends now.
- [ ] Decide what to do with the **house** (sale, rental, handover) and confirm the dates with the notaire or agent.

## Week 4 (7–13 Dec): Paperwork in Portugal
- [ ] Get a **NIF** (Portuguese tax number) if you don't have one. You need it for almost everything, including utilities, a bank account, and a phone contract.
- [ ] Confirm with your Porto landlord that **electricity, water, and internet** will be on by 15 January, or arrange them yourself.
- [ ] Find out where to register at the **SNS** (health centre) and where the nearest *Junta de Freguesia* is.

## Week 5 (14–20 Dec): Notices and cancellations
- [ ] Give notice for **electricity, gas, water, internet, and phone** in Lyon, effective just after the movers leave.
- [ ] Cancel or transfer **home insurance** from the day after you hand over the house.
- [ ] Set up **mail forwarding to Portugal** with La Poste (*réexpédition internationale*).
- [ ] Change your address with your pension funds, mutuelle, and any subscriptions.
- [ ] If the movers aren't packing everything, **arrange help** (family, a neighbour, or a paid packer for a day).

## Weeks 6 (21 Dec–3 Jan): Holidays, kept light on purpose
- [ ] Enjoy the holidays and say your goodbyes.
- [ ] Gently set aside **small items** like books, photos, and papers. Only fill boxes to a weight you can comfortably move, or leave them for the packers.
- [ ] Final collection of unsold furniture.

## Week 7 (4–10 Jan): Final preparations
- [ ] Re-confirm the date, time, and Porto address with the movers.
- [ ] Pack an **"open first" suitcase** that travels **with you**, not in the truck:
  - Passport/ID, S1 form, NIF, rental contract, house sale documents
  - Medication and prescriptions
  - Phone, chargers, glasses
  - A few days of clothes, bedding, towels, a kettle, mug, and toilet paper
- [ ] Book your own travel to Porto, ideally arriving a day before the truck.
- [ ] Photograph valuable items before packing, for insurance purposes.

## Week 8 (11–15 Jan): Moving week
- [ ] Movers pack and load. Your job is to **point, not lift.**
- [ ] Do the final house walk-through, take **meter readings**, and photograph them.
- [ ] Hand over the keys.
- [ ] **15 January:** Arrive in Porto. Check items against the movers' inventory before you sign anything, and note any damage on the form.

---

## After you arrive (first 3 months)
- Register your residence at the **Câmara Municipal** (the *CRUE* certificate for EU citizens staying more than 3 months)
- Register with the **SNS** health centre using your S1
- Open a Portuguese bank account if useful

---

**One tip for calm:** The only things that are truly urgent this week are **measuring the flat and booking the movers.** Everything else can wait its turn.

If you tell me your nationality and whether you're selling or renting out the Lyon house, I can adjust the paperwork steps. I can also turn this into a printable one-page version.

# Sponsored Walk: Will We Reach the Infusion Pump Target?

## Short answer
**No, not yet.** With 38 walkers at the minimum pledge, we would fall **96,000 shillings short**. We need **39 more walkers, 77 in total**, to buy the 150,000-shilling infusion pump.

## Where we stand now

| Item | Amount (shillings) |
|---|---|
| 38 walkers × 2,500 minimum pledge | 95,000 |
| Less venue and T-shirts | −41,000 |
| **Net raised** | **54,000** |
| Target (infusion pump) | 150,000 |
| **Shortfall** | **96,000** |

## How many more walkers we need
- Each extra walker adds 2,500 shillings.
- 96,000 ÷ 2,500 = 38.4, which rounds up to **39 more walkers**.

**Check with 77 walkers:** 77 × 2,500 = 192,500 − 41,000 = **151,500**. This hits the target with 1,500 to spare.

With 76 walkers we would reach only 149,000, which is 1,000 short. So 77 walkers is the minimum.

## Another way to close the gap
If we keep the 38 walkers we have, each would need to raise an average of **5,027 shillings** instead of 2,500. That is (150,000 + 41,000) ÷ 38, rounded up. A mix of both approaches also works. For example, every walker who raises more than 2,500 reduces the number of new walkers we need.

## One thing to confirm
These figures assume the 41,000-shilling cost stays the same no matter how many people join. If the T-shirt order grows with each new walker, each extra T-shirt cuts into that walker's 2,500. In that case we would need a few more than 39 extra walkers. Check with the T-shirt supplier whether the 41,000 covers additional shirts.

# Lesson Plan: The Water Cycle (Grade 4)

**Duration:** 50 minutes
**Class size:** 42 pupils (7 groups of 6)
**Resources:** Blackboard, chalk, and a few items from home

## Learning Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils will be able to:
1. Name the four main stages of the water cycle: **evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection**.
2. Explain in simple words what happens at each stage.
3. Put the stages in the correct order and explain why the cycle repeats.

## Materials to Bring

- 1 flask or jug of **hot water** (hot, not boiling, for safety)
- 1 clear glass or jar
- 1 small plate or saucer to cover the jar
- A few **ice cubes** in a small container or cloth (cold water works if you have no ice)
- **7 sets of paper cards** prepared before class. Each set has 4 cards: EVAPORATION, CONDENSATION, PRECIPITATION, COLLECTION. Scrap paper is fine.
- Optional: 1 wet cloth and a sunny window to show drying

## Blackboard Preparation (before class)

Draw a large simple picture: **sun** in the top corner, **sea or river** at the bottom, a **hill or mountain** on one side, and **clouds** at the top. Leave space for arrows and labels, which you will add during the lesson.

## Lesson Procedure

### 1. Introduction / Hook (5 minutes)

- Ask: *"When your mother hangs wet clothes outside, they become dry. Where does the water go?"*
- Take 3 or 4 answers. Accept all ideas without correcting yet.
- Ask: *"Where does rain come from?"*
- Say: *"Today we will find out that the water you drank this morning may once have been in the sea, in a cloud, or even in a dinosaur's river! Water travels in a circle. We call it the **water cycle**."*

### 2. Teacher Demonstration (8 minutes)

Do this on the front desk so all pupils can see. Invite pupils to come forward row by row to look closely if space allows.

1. Pour hot water into the clear jar (about one third full).
2. Cover the jar with the plate and put the ice on top of the plate.
3. Wait 2 to 3 minutes. While waiting, ask: *"What do you think will happen?"*
4. Lift the plate and show the **water drops** underneath. Let a few drops fall back into the jar.

Explain while pointing:
- Hot water → rising steam = **evaporation** (the sun heats water)
- Drops forming under the cold plate = **condensation** (clouds forming)
- Drops falling back = **precipitation** (rain)
- Water back in the jar = **collection** (rivers, lakes, seas)

### 3. Blackboard Explanation (10 minutes)

Using your drawing, add arrows and labels one at a time. Write a short definition under each and have pupils say each word aloud together.

| Stage | Simple Explanation | Board Arrow |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaporation** | The sun heats water. It turns into invisible water vapour and rises. | From sea up to sky |
| **Condensation** | High up it is cold. Vapour cools and turns into tiny drops that make clouds. | Into the clouds |
| **Precipitation** | Drops join, get heavy, and fall as rain, hail, or snow. | From clouds down to hill |
| **Collection** | Water gathers in rivers, lakes, seas, and under the ground. Then it starts again. | From hill down to sea |

**Memory aid:** Teach this chant, with actions:
> *"Sun heats it up (arms rise) — Evaporation!
> Cools in the sky (hug yourself) — Condensation!
> Falls back down (wiggle fingers down) — Precipitation!
> Gathers below (sweep arms low) — Collection!"*

Repeat it twice with the whole class. It also gives pupils a chance to move.

**Pupils copy** the diagram and the four words into their exercise books (allow about 4 minutes of this time).

### 4. Group Activity: "Water Drop's Journey" (15 minutes)

**Organising 42 pupils:** Form 7 groups of 6 by having pupils turn to the desks behind them. Give each group one set of 4 cards.

**Part A: Sequencing (5 minutes)**
- Groups shuffle the cards and arrange them in the correct order in a circle on the desk.
- Each group must decide **which stage comes after Collection** (answer: Evaporation again, which is why it is a *cycle*).
- Walk around and check. Groups that finish raise their hands.

**Part B: Act It Out (10 minutes)**
- In each group, 4 pupils each hold one card and act out their stage. The other 2 pupils are **narrators** who tell the story of a water drop: *"I was a drop in the sea. The sun heated me and..."*
- Give 4 minutes to practise.
- Call **3 or 4 groups** (time will not allow all 7) to present to the class in about 1 minute each. Tell the remaining groups they will present in the next lesson so everyone feels included.

**Classroom management tips for a large class:**
- Set a clear signal for silence, such as a raised hand or a clap pattern, before starting.
- Appoint one **group leader** per group to collect and return cards.
- Write the time limit on the board.

### 5. Quiz (7 minutes)

Write the questions on the board, or read them aloud slowly. Pupils answer in their exercise books individually.

**Quiz: The Water Cycle**

1. What is it called when the sun heats water and it turns into vapour and rises?
   a) Precipitation  b) Evaporation  c) Collection
2. What are clouds made of?
   a) Smoke  b) Cotton  c) Tiny drops of water
3. Name **one** type of precipitation.
4. Where does water collect after it rains? Give **one** example.
5. True or False: The water cycle stops after it rains once.

Pupils can swap books with a neighbour and mark each other's work as you read out the answers. This saves you time.

**Answer Key**
1. b) Evaporation
2. c) Tiny drops of water
3. Rain, snow, hail, or sleet (any one)
4. River, lake, sea, ocean, pond, or underground (any one)
5. False. The cycle repeats again and again.

### 6. Closing (5 minutes)

- Ask a few pupils: *"Tell me one thing you learned today."*
- Return to the opening question: *"So where did the water from the wet clothes go?"* (It evaporated into the air and will become part of a cloud.)
- Do the chant one final time.

**Homework (optional):** Draw and label the water cycle at home, and find one example of evaporation or condensation in the home. Examples: steam from cooking, drops on a cold cup, wet floor drying.

## Timing Summary

| Section | Time |
|---|---|
| Introduction | 5 min |
| Demonstration | 8 min |
| Blackboard explanation + copying | 10 min |
| Group activity | 15 min |
| Quiz + peer marking | 7 min |
| Closing | 5 min |
| **Total** | **50 min** |

## Notes for the Teacher

- **Safety:** Carry the hot water yourself and keep pupils at a safe distance during the demonstration.
- **No ice?** A metal plate cooled in cold water still works, but more slowly. You can also start the demonstration at the very beginning of the lesson so the drops have more time to form.
- **Running short on time?** Shorten Part B of the group activity to 2 group presentations.
- **For faster learners:** Ask them to explain where the sun's role fits in, or why sea water is salty but rain is not. When water evaporates, the salt stays behind.

| Powder cost per cup | ¥95 | ¥114 (+¥19) | ¥114 |
| Price | ¥580 | ¥580 | ¥600 |

## Why ¥600 works for regulars

- **It's small.** It's a 3.4% increase, and most people won't notice ¥20 on a drink they already enjoy.
- **It's a round number.** ¥600 is easy to pay and remember, and paying with coins is easier for older customers.
- **It's fair.** You're passing on your cost, not adding profit, and regulars tend to sense that.
- **It's well timed.** Prices often change in January, so it won't feel unusual.

## When you might go higher (¥620–650)

Consider a bigger rise if your **milk, cups, rent, or wages** have also gone up, or will soon. Then one modest rise now is better than two small ones in quick succession, which can annoy regulars more than a single change. Check your full cost per cup before deciding.

## How to introduce it gently

1. **Put up a short, honest notice** a couple of weeks ahead. For example: 「1月より抹茶の仕入れ価格が上がるため、抹茶ラテを600円に改定させていただきます。いつもありがとうございます。」 Regulars appreciate being told rather than surprised.
2. **Thank them personally.** A word at the counter goes a long way with neighbourhood customers.
3. **Consider a small loyalty gesture**, such as a stamp card (e.g. 10th drink free). It costs little and makes regulars feel valued.
4. **Keep the quality the same.** Don't quietly use less matcha to save money. Regulars notice taste changes more than ¥20.

## Alternatives if you really don't want to raise prices
- **Absorb it**, if your margins are comfortable and the latte mostly brings people in for other items.
- **Get quotes from other suppliers**, though switching may change the taste.
- **Offer a smaller size** at ¥580 and price the regular at ¥600, so price-sensitive customers have a choice.

Overall, a ¥20 increase to ¥600 with a friendly notice is the low-risk option that keeps both your margin and your regulars intact.

# 12 Calm Days in Lisbon in March

## Before you plan, three things to know

- **Lisbon is very hilly and paved with cobblestones**, which get slippery in March rain. This plan uses trams, the metro, ferries and taxis (Bolt or Uber, usually €6–10 per ride in the centre) so your walking stays near or under 2 km a day.
- **Stay somewhere flat.** Good areas are Baixa, Avenidas Novas, Campo de Ourique, or Parque das Nações. Avoid Alfama and Bairro Alto, which are lovely but steep. Many old buildings have no lift, so ask for a lift or the ground floor.
- **Ask for senior discounts.** Many museums and monuments give reduced entry at 65+, so bring your passport.

## Budget (about 4.3 zł = €1)

| Item | Euros | Złoty |
|---|---|---|
| Accommodation, 11 nights × ~€65 (guesthouse or small apartment) | €715 | ~3,075 zł |
| Food, ~€30/day (pastries and coffee are cheap; lunch "prato do dia" ~€10–12) | €360 | ~1,550 zł |
| Taxis, public transport, airport transfers | €120 | ~515 zł |
| Sights and entry tickets | €90 | ~385 zł |
| Buffer (pharmacy, gifts, a fado evening) | €100 | ~430 zł |
| **Total** | **~€1,385** | **~5,955 zł** |

If you stay with your daughter, you save about 3,000 zł and the budget becomes very comfortable. Prices are estimates, so check current ones closer to March.

## Day-by-day plan

**Day 1 – Arrival.** Take a taxi from the airport (about €15–20, 20 minutes) rather than the metro, which has stairs and transfers. Settle in, rest, and have a relaxed dinner with your daughter nearby. *Walking: under 0.5 km.*

**Day 2 – Baixa and the river.** Take a taxi to Praça do Comércio, a large flat square on the river. Have coffee at Martinho da Arcada, the city's oldest café. Then sit on the riverside steps at Ribeira das Naus. The Baixa streets are flat and good for a short stroll. *About 1.5 km.*

**Day 3 – Belém.** Take tram 15 from Praça da Figueira (it's flat and has seats). Visit the Jerónimos Monastery and have the famous pastéis de Belém across the street. Admire the Belém Tower from a riverside bench rather than walking the extra 1 km to it. Take a taxi home. *About 1.5–2 km.*

**Day 4 – Rest day.** Have a slow morning and spend the day in your daughter's neighbourhood. A local market such as Mercado de Campo de Ourique is good for lunch with seating. *Under 1 km.*

**Day 5 – Gulbenkian Museum and garden.** This is a world-class museum, quiet and fully accessible, with a peaceful garden full of benches and ducks. It's a short taxi ride, or take the metro to São Sebastião, which has lifts. *About 1.5 km.*

**Day 6 – Tram 28 through the old town.** Board early (before 9:30) at Martim Moniz to get a seat. It climbs through Graça and Alfama, so you see the hills without climbing them. Get off at Miradouro de Santa Luzia for the view, then take a taxi back down. *About 1 km.*

**Day 7 – Cascais by the sea.** Take the train from Cais do Sodré, about 40 minutes along the coast for roughly €2.50 each way. Cascais has a flat seaside promenade, fish restaurants, and benches facing the ocean. *About 1.5–2 km at your own pace.*

**Day 8 – Rest, then a fado evening.** Rest during the day. In the evening, go to a small fado house in Alfama with dinner (about €40–60). Take a taxi door to door so the hills don't matter. *Under 0.5 km.*

**Day 9 – Parque das Nações.** This modern district is completely flat. Visit the Oceanário (one of Europe's best aquariums), then ride the cable car along the river. Take the metro to Oriente, which has lifts. *About 1.5 km.*

**Day 10 – Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo).** It's set in a beautiful old convent with a gilded chapel, has a pleasant café in the cloister, and is rarely crowded. Take a taxi both ways. *About 1 km.*

**Day 11 – Ferry across the river.** Take the ferry from Cais do Sodré to Cacilhas (10 minutes, about €1.50), which gives lovely views of Lisbon from the water. Have a seafood lunch at a riverside restaurant, then ferry back. *About 1–1.5 km.*

**Day 12 – Departure.** Have a slow breakfast and buy last gifts nearby (tinned sardines, tiles, and pastries travel well). Take a taxi to the airport and allow plenty of time. *Minimal walking.*

## Practical tips for your knee

- **Shoes:** wear shoes with good rubber grip, because the polished cobblestones are slippery even when dry.
- **Walking pole:** consider a folding walking stick or pole for the hills and stairs.
- **Transport card:** buy a Viva Viagem card (€0.50) at any metro station and load it with credit for trams, metro, trains and ferries.
- **Rest days:** swap days 4 and 8 freely if your knee needs a break earlier.
- **Weather:** March is usually 15–18°C with some rain, so bring a light waterproof jacket.
- **Sintra:** it's famous but very hilly and crowded. I left it out, but it could work with a private driver if your daughter wants to splurge.

Will you be staying with your daughter or in your own accommodation? If you're staying with her, I can rebalance the budget toward a few special extras, like a nice dinner out or a day trip by car.

# Your 8-Week Moving Plan: Lyon → Porto, Friday 15 January 2027

**Today is Wednesday 18 November, so you have 58 days.** Two things make this plan more urgent than it looks:

- **Christmas and New Year fall in weeks 6 and 7.** Movers, charities and administrations slow down then, so the heavy decisions need to happen in **November and early December**.
- **Your back rules out lifting anything heavy.** Every step that involves lifting, carrying or dismantling below is assigned to someone else: the movers, buyers, charities or paid helpers.

---

## The big decision: half truck (1,600 €) or full truck (2,800 €)

For a **52 m² flat**, the **half truck at 1,600 €** is almost certainly enough, and it saves you **1,200 €**. That saving can pay for the movers to pack for you, so you don't strain your back.

Before you book, ask the moving company these questions in writing:

1. What volume (in m³) does "half a truck" mean, and can someone do a visit or video call to check your list fits?
2. Does the 1,600 € include **packing, loading, unloading, and reassembling** furniture, or only transport?
3. What is the **packing service price** (cartons + packing by their staff)?
4. What **insurance** is included, and up to what value?
5. Have they planned for **Porto access**: parking authorisation for the truck, narrow streets, stairs or lift at your building?
6. What is the **delivery date in Porto**? (Lyon–Porto is about 1,500 km, so the truck may arrive a day or more after loading.)
7. What happens if you have slightly more than half a truck?

---

## Week 1: Wed 18 – Tue 24 November · *Decide and book*

- [ ] Get the **floor plan or exact measurements** of the Porto flat: each room, wall lengths, door widths, lift size if there is one. Ask the landlord or agent by email.
- [ ] Walk through your Lyon house and make **three lists**: *Comes to Porto* / *Sell or give* / *Throw away*.
- [ ] Keep the "Comes to Porto" list to what fits 52 m²: bed, one sofa or armchair, small table and chairs, one wardrobe or chest of drawers, kitchen basics, personal belongings.
- [ ] Send the 7 questions above to the movers.
- [ ] **Book the movers this week**, ideally the half truck with their packing service. Agree on the loading date (e.g. Tuesday 12 or Wednesday 13 January) and the Porto delivery date.
- [ ] Book your own **journey to Porto** for 14 or 15 January, so you arrive before the furniture.

## Week 2: Wed 25 November – Tue 1 December · *Get rid of furniture*

- [ ] Photograph furniture you'll sell and post it on **Leboncoin**. Write "*à venir chercher sur place, l'acheteur démonte et porte*" (buyer collects and carries).
- [ ] Contact **Emmaüs** or a **ressourcerie** in Lyon to book a **free collection** of furniture you can't sell. Book now, because December slots fill up.
- [ ] For broken or unusable items, book a **bulky item collection (encombrants)** with the Métropole de Lyon, or pay a junk removal service. Do not take things to the déchèterie yourself.
- [ ] Ask a neighbour, family member or paid helper (e.g. through a local odd-jobs service) to be present for collections, if you'd rather not be alone with strangers.

## Week 3: Wed 2 – Tue 8 December · *Paperwork, France side*

- [ ] **Pension funds**: tell the Assurance retraite and Agirc-Arrco (or your other funds) your new address and moving date. Ask whether you need to change bank accounts.
- [ ] **Health**: if your pension is French, ask your **CPAM** for the **S1 form**. It lets you register with Portugal's public health system.
- [ ] **Medicines**: see your doctor. Ask for **2–3 months of prescriptions**, a summary of your medical file, and a letter about your back condition (useful for a new doctor in Porto).
- [ ] **Taxes**: inform your tax office (impots.gouv.fr, "Gérer mon prélèvement à la source / Signaler un changement d'adresse") that you're moving abroad on 15 January 2027. Because the rules depend on your type of pension, ask a tax adviser before March whether your pensions will be taxed in France or Portugal.
- [ ] **Mail**: order **international permanent mail forwarding** from La Poste, starting 15 January.

## Week 4: Wed 9 – Tue 15 December · *Paperwork, Portugal side*

- [ ] Get a **NIF** (Portuguese tax number) if you don't have one yet. You need it for the lease, bank, electricity and internet. It can be done online through a representative or at a Finanças office.
- [ ] Check with the Porto landlord that **electricity, water and internet** will be on by 15 January, or set them up now.
- [ ] Confirm with the landlord: **key handover time on 15 January**, building access, and whether the truck needs parking permission from the **Câmara Municipal do Porto** (and who requests it, you, the landlord or the movers).
- [ ] Look up the **Centro de Saúde** (health centre) nearest your flat, where you'll register with the S1 form.

## Week 5: Wed 16 – Tue 22 December · *Cancel contracts in Lyon*

- [ ] Give notice for **electricity and gas, water, internet/box, phone landline** effective 15 January. Ask for a final meter reading that day.
- [ ] **Home insurance**: cancel effective the day you leave (moving is a legal reason to cancel). Arrange insurance for the Porto flat starting 15 January.
- [ ] Cancel or transfer **subscriptions**: newspapers, gym, cleaning help, etc.
- [ ] Return the internet box (ask if they'll send prepaid packaging).
- [ ] Check that all Leboncoin and Emmaüs collections are done or booked before 31 December.

## Week 6: Wed 23 – Tue 29 December · *Christmas, light week*

- [ ] Rest. Nothing urgent is planned for this week on purpose.
- [ ] Sort **papers and photos** sitting down: keep important documents, shred the rest.
- [ ] Put **all important documents in one folder** that travels **with you**, not in the truck: ID/passport, Porto lease, NIF, S1 form, prescriptions, medical summary, bank cards, movers' contract, insurance papers.

## Week 7: Wed 30 December – Tue 5 January · *Final clear-out*

- [ ] Confirm with the movers by phone: **date, time, address, Porto delivery date**, and that packing is included.
- [ ] Final check of the "Comes to Porto" list against the Porto floor plan.
- [ ] Anything still unsold: give it to Emmaüs, neighbours, or the encombrants collection. Don't pay to move furniture that won't fit.
- [ ] Tell your bank your new address. Keep your French account open until pension payments are settled.

## Week 8: Wed 6 – Tue 12 January · *Pack your survival bag*

- [ ] Pack a **wheeled suitcase that travels with you**, for the gap before the truck arrives:
  - 1 week of clothes, toiletries, **all medicines** plus prescriptions
  - Phone charger, glasses, important documents folder
  - Bedsheets, a towel, a few kitchen items (mug, plate, cutlery, kettle if small)
  - Back support: cushion, heat patch, painkillers you normally use
- [ ] Label which room each item goes into in Porto (bedroom / kitchen / living room), or ask the movers to do it.
- [ ] Book a cleaning service for the Lyon house after loading, if you need to leave it clean.
- [ ] **Loading day** (the date agreed with the movers): your job is only to point and supervise. Do not carry anything.

## Final days: Wed 13 – Fri 15 January · *Leave and arrive*

- [ ] After the truck leaves: walk through every room, cupboard and the cellar or garden shed.
- [ ] Take **meter readings with photos** (electricity, gas, water).
- [ ] Hand over or secure the house keys.
- [ ] **Friday 15 January**: travel to Porto, collect your keys, check electricity, water and heating work, and sleep with your survival bag.
- [ ] On delivery day: tell the movers where everything goes, have them **reassemble the bed first**, and check for damage before signing.

## After arrival (first 3 months in Porto)

- [ ] Register at the **Centro de Saúde** with your S1 form.
- [ ] If you're an EU citizen, apply for the **certificado de registo** (residence certificate) at the Câmara Municipal within 3 months of arriving. If you're not, check your visa or residence permit steps with AIMA.
- [ ] Send your new Porto address to pension funds, bank and the French tax office.

---

**The three most important things to do this week:** measure the Porto flat, book the half truck with packing included, and book the Emmaüs collection. Everything after that is paperwork you can do sitting down.

# Lesson Plan: The Water Cycle

**Class:** Grade 4 · **Pupils:** 42 · **Duration:** 50 minutes
**Resources available:** Blackboard, chalk, and items from home (no projector, no internet)

## Learning Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils will be able to:
1. Name the four stages of the water cycle: **evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection**.
2. Explain in simple words what happens to water at each stage.
3. Explain that the Sun's heat drives the water cycle.

## Materials to Bring from Home

**For the teacher demonstration:**
- 1 flask of hot water (not boiling)
- 1 clear glass bowl or large clear jar
- 1 metal plate or metal pot lid big enough to cover the bowl
- 6–8 ice cubes in a small container or wrapped in a cloth
- 1 small cloth for spills

**For the group activity:**
- 7 sets of 4 word cards, cut from cardboard boxes or old notebook covers. Each set has: **EVAPORATION**, **CONDENSATION**, **PRECIPITATION**, **COLLECTION**. That is 28 cards in total.
- 7 sheets of paper (any scrap paper, used on one side)
- 7 pencils or crayons
- 7 small rubber bands or paper clips to keep each card set together

**Before class:** Write the cards at home and bundle them into 7 sets. Draw the blackboard diagram (below) before pupils arrive if you can. It saves about 5 minutes.

## Blackboard Layout

Draw this on the left two-thirds of the board:

```
              ☀ SUN
                 \
        ☁ ☁ ☁     \        (2) CONDENSATION
       CLOUDS      \        water vapour cools → tiny drops → clouds
      /      ↑      \
     ↓       |       
  (3) PRECIPITATION   (1) EVAPORATION
  rain, hail, snow     Sun heats water → water vapour rises
     ↓       |
  ⛰ hills    |
     ↓       |
  ~~~~~~ RIVER → LAKE → SEA ~~~~~~
        (4) COLLECTION
   water gathers in rivers, lakes, seas, underground
```

Use the right third of the board for the quiz later. Keep it empty for now.

## Lesson Procedure

### 1. Hook and Introduction (0–5 minutes)

Ask the class:
> "When it rains, the ground is wet. The next afternoon, the puddles are gone. Where did the water go?"

Take 3–4 answers. Accept all ideas without correcting yet.

Then say:
> "Today we will follow one drop of water on its journey. It goes up into the sky and comes back down, again and again. This journey is called **the water cycle**."

Write **THE WATER CYCLE** in large letters at the top of the board.

### 2. Teaching the Four Stages (5–17 minutes)

Point to each part of the blackboard diagram as you explain. After each stage, have the whole class repeat the word aloud twice. With 42 pupils, choral repetition keeps everyone involved.

**Stage 1: Evaporation (3 minutes)**
- "The Sun heats water in seas, rivers, lakes and puddles."
- "The water turns into an invisible gas called **water vapour** and rises into the air."
- Everyday example: "Wet clothes on the line become dry. The water evaporated."
- **Action:** Pupils wiggle their fingers upward, slowly raising their hands. Water is rising.

**Stage 2: Condensation (3 minutes)**
- "High in the sky the air is cold. The water vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water."
- "Millions of these tiny drops together make **clouds**."
- Everyday example: "When you breathe on a cold mirror or a cold glass, it becomes foggy. That is condensation."
- **Action:** Pupils bring their hands together above their heads in a round cloud shape.

**Stage 3: Precipitation (3 minutes)**
- "The tiny drops join together and become big and heavy. The cloud cannot hold them, so they fall."
- "Water falling from clouds is called **precipitation**. It can be rain, hail or snow."
- **Action:** Pupils tap their fingers on their desks, softly at first and then faster, like rain.

**Stage 4: Collection (3 minutes)**
- "The water falls on land and flows into rivers, lakes and seas. Some soaks into the ground."
- "This is called **collection**. Then the Sun heats the water again, and the cycle starts again."
- **Action:** Pupils move their hands in a wavy motion, like a river.

**Quick check:** Do all four actions in order while the class calls out the words: *Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation, Collection.* Do it twice, the second time faster.

### 3. Teacher Demonstration: "A Water Cycle in a Bowl" (17–24 minutes)

Place the bowl on the front desk. Ask pupils to stay in their seats. Pupils at the back may stand quietly to see.

1. Pour hot water from the flask into the clear bowl until it is about one-third full. Say: *"This is the sea. The hot water is like water heated by the Sun."* Steam will be visible. Ask: **"Which stage is this?"** (Evaporation)
2. Cover the bowl with the metal plate or lid and put the ice cubes on top. Say: *"The ice makes the plate cold, like the cold air high in the sky."*
3. Wait 2–3 minutes. Walk slowly along the rows holding the bowl at eye level so pupils can see the droplets forming under the plate. Ask: **"What is forming under the plate? Which stage is this?"** (Condensation)
4. Lift the plate carefully and tilt it so pupils see drops falling back into the bowl. Ask: **"Which stage is this?"** (Precipitation)
5. Point to the water gathered in the bowl. Ask: **"And now?"** (Collection)

**Safety:** Only you handle the hot water. Keep the flask out of pupils' reach.

### 4. Group Activity: "The Water Drop Journey" (24–39 minutes)

**Grouping (2 minutes):** Divide the class into **7 groups of 6 pupils**. Use desks that are next to each other so pupils only turn their chairs. Do not move furniture.

Give each group a job for every member:

| Role | Job |
|---|---|
| **Leader** | Keeps the group on task |
| **Card Keeper** | Holds and arranges the 4 cards |
| **Artist 1** | Draws the Sun and the sea |
| **Artist 2** | Draws clouds and rain |
| **Writer** | Writes the labels on the drawing |
| **Speaker** | Presents the group's work to the class |

**Instructions (write these short steps on the board or say them clearly):**

1. **Step 1 (3 minutes):** Put your 4 cards in the correct order to show the water's journey. Put them in a circle, because the cycle never ends.
2. **Step 2 (7 minutes):** On your paper, draw the water cycle. Include the Sun, the sea, clouds, rain and a river. Draw arrows to show where the water goes. Label each stage with its word.
3. **Step 3:** Each group writes **one sentence** at the bottom of the paper: *"Without the Sun, the water cycle would stop because…"*

**While groups work:** Walk around the room. Check each group's card order and ask the Speaker: *"Where does the water go after condensation?"*

**Sharing (3 minutes):** Choose **2 groups** to share. Their Speaker holds up the drawing and reads the group's sentence. Praise correct arrows and labels. Collect all 7 papers at the end to display on the classroom wall.

**Time signal:** Raise your hand and count down "5, 4, 3, 2, 1, hands up." Pupils stop, raise a hand, and go quiet. Practise it once at the start of the activity.

### 5. Quiz (39–47 minutes)

Pupils return to facing the front and write the answers in their exercise books individually. Write the questions on the right third of the board while they settle, or read each question aloud twice.

**Water Cycle Quiz**

1. What gives the heat that makes water evaporate?
2. When water vapour cools high in the sky and makes clouds, what is this stage called?
3. Name **two** kinds of precipitation.
4. Write the four stages of the water cycle in the correct order, starting with evaporation.
5. After it rains, where does the water collect? Name **two** places.

**Answer Key**

1. The Sun
2. Condensation
3. Any two of: rain, hail, snow (sleet is also acceptable)
4. Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → Collection
5. Any two of: rivers, lakes, seas/oceans, ponds, underground/in the soil

### 6. Marking and Wrap-Up (47–50 minutes)

- Pupils swap books with the pupil next to them.
- Read the answers aloud. Partners give a tick for each correct answer.
- Ask: *"Hands up if you got 5 out of 5… 4… 3."* This shows you quickly which pupils need help next lesson.
- **Closing question:** *"The water you drank today may have been rain on a mountain long ago. Why is that possible?"* (Because the same water keeps going around the cycle.)

## Homework (optional)

Tonight, find **one example of evaporation or condensation at home**, such as steam from a cooking pot, a wet floor drying, or drops on a cold cup. Write one sentence about it and draw a small picture.

## Assessment Notes

- **Group activity:** Check that the card order and the arrows on each drawing are correct.
- **Quiz:** Pupils scoring 3 or fewer out of 5 should get a quick review of the four stages at the start of the next lesson, using the hand actions.

QC still pays about ₱69 more for each day you work, even with the sixth day. It also has no commute time, while Makati's daily commute adds unpaid hours.

**The trade-off**

Makati gives you 52 more days off a year. You'd be giving up ₱114,000 to get them, which works out to about **₱2,192 for each extra day off**.

**Bottom line:** On money alone, Quezon City wins clearly. Makati only makes sense if having one more free day each week is worth more than ₱2,192 a day to you.

**Exchange rate used:** about **4.25 zł per €1**. Check the current rate before you go.

**Lisbon is very hilly**, with slippery stone pavements. So this plan keeps you in the flat areas (Baixa, the riverside, Belém, Avenidas Novas, Parque das Nações). It uses trams, the metro, escalators and cheap Bolt or Uber taxis for every slope.

# Chess Club Night: Wednesday 18:00–20:00

**The core problem:** 6 boards seat 12 players, so 2 people are always without a board. Every activity below either uses all 14 people or gives the extras something useful to do.

## Schedule

**18:00–18:15 | Welcome & sort-out (15 min)**
- Quick intros: name, and a self-rating from 0 to 3 (0 = never played, 3 = plays regularly).
- Split into **Beginners (~7)** and **Experienced (~7)**.
- Mention plans for future meetings and ask people to bring boards if they have one (this solves next week's problem).

**18:15–18:50 | Buddy session (35 min)**
- Pair each experienced player with a beginner: **6 boards, 12 people.**
- Experienced players teach piece movement, then play a "talk-through" game, explaining their thinking out loud.
- **The 2 extras:** they become a *team* on one board, or they rotate in by swapping with a pair every 10–15 min. Alternatively, an organizer (you) takes them through a mini-lesson on checkmate patterns on a spare surface or a phone/tablet.

**18:50–19:00 | Break (10 min)**
Snacks, chatting, reset boards. Good moment for people to swap partners.

**19:00–19:40 | Team chess / Consultation games (40 min)**
- Play **2v2 or 3v3** on each board: teammates discuss each move before playing it.
- Mix the teams so each one has a beginner and an experienced player.
- With 14 people: e.g. 4 boards of 2v2 (16 seats, so a couple of boards have 1v2 or use a 3-person team). This format **seats everyone at once** and gets beginners talking about chess instead of just watching.

**19:40–19:55 | Mini-tournament or Bughouse (15 min)**
Choose based on the room's energy:
- **Bughouse** (teams of 2, two boards per 4 players): chaotic, loud, very fun. 3 games use all 6 boards and 12 people; rotate the 2 extras in after each game, since games are short.
- **Blitz "king of the hill"** for experienced players (5-min games, winner stays), while beginners play each other with an experienced player floating between boards to help.

**19:55–20:00 | Wrap-up (5 min)**
- Ask what they liked and what they want next time (lessons? tournaments? casual play?).
- Collect contact details / set up a group chat.
- Announce the next meeting.

## Tips
- **Download a chess app** (Lichess is free) so anyone without a board can play phone-to-phone. That effectively gives you unlimited "boards."
- **Expect fewer than 14.** Sign-up numbers usually drop, so you may end up with all 12 seats filled and no extras.
- **Have a printed cheat sheet** of piece movements for beginners. It frees up the experienced players.
- **Don't run a strict tournament on night one.** Beginners losing badly repeatedly is the fastest way to lose members.

Good luck with the club!

# A Realistic Walking Plan to Reach 8,000 Steps

Your split shift helps here. The 10am–3pm gap is a good window for walking. Walking for 10–15 minutes **after meals** is also one of the most effective things you can do for blood sugar, so the plan is built around your mealtimes.

**Rough guide:** 10 minutes of steady walking is about 1,000 steps.

## Build Up Gradually (8 Weeks)

Jumping from 3,000 to 8,000 straight away is a common way to aggravate a dodgy knee. Add about 750 steps a day each fortnight or so:

| Weeks | Daily target | Extra walking vs now |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | 4,500 | ~15 min |
| 3–4 | 6,000 | ~30 min |
| 5–6 | 7,000 | ~40 min |
| 7–8 | 8,000 | ~50 min |

If your knee complains, stay at the current level for an extra week before moving up.

## Your Daily Routine at 8,000 Steps

| Time | What | Steps |
|---|---|---|
| Before 6am | Park or get dropped a bit further from the depot (5 min each way) | ~500 |
| During shift | At layovers or terminus stops, walk 3–5 min around the bus or stop | ~500–800 |
| 10:15am | Short walk after your shift or with a snack, 10 min | ~1,000 |
| 12:30–1pm | **After lunch**: 15–20 min walk (the most important one) | ~1,500–2,000 |
| 2:30pm | Walk to the depot or a loop before clocking back on, 10 min | ~1,000 |
| After 7pm | Park further away on the way home (5 min) | ~500 |
| ~8pm | **After dinner**: 15 min easy walk | ~1,500 |
| Day-to-day | Normal moving around | ~1,500 |

That totals about 8,000. If a day goes wrong, prioritise the two after-meal walks.

**Early weeks version (4,500):** Do the after-lunch walk (10 min) and the after-dinner walk (5–10 min), and leave out the rest.

## Looking After Your Knee

- **Keep it flat.** Choose canal paths, parks, seafronts, or a shopping centre on wet days.
- **Use several short walks rather than one long one.** That's easier on the joint, and it's why the plan uses 10–15 minute chunks.
- **Wear supportive, cushioned shoes**, not your work shoes if they're flat-soled.
- **Watch how it responds.** Mild ache that settles by the next day is usually fine. Swelling, sharp pain, or limping means you should drop back a level.
- **Take stairs and kerbs carefully.** Step up with your good leg and down with the sore one.
- If the knee keeps limiting you, ask your GP about a **physio referral**. Simple strengthening exercises can make walking much easier.

## Other Tips

- **Track your steps** with your phone or a cheap pedometer. Seeing the number go up helps you stick with it.
- **Check with your doctor if you take insulin or gliclazide-type tablets**, since extra activity can drop your sugar too low. Carry a sugary snack just in case.
- **Rest days are fine.** Hitting 8,000 on 5 days a week is still a big win.
- **Wear hi-vis or carry a light** for early or dark evening walks this time of year.

# Your Overdraft Payoff Schedule: Clear £1,800 by November 2027

**Your facts:** £1,800 overdrawn at 39.9% EAR. You can pay £150 a month, plus your £400 bonus on 20 December 2026.

**Result:** The overdraft is cleared in **November 2027**, 12 months from now. The total cost is **£2,064.81**, of which **£264.81 is interest**.

## How the £150 has to work

Your overdraft goes down only if the £150 **stays in your current account**. If you move it to a savings pot, the overdraft won't shrink and the interest keeps running. In practice, "paying" means leaving £150 more in the account each month than you did before, so your lowest point each month is £150 higher.

## The schedule

39.9% EAR works out to about **2.84% interest per month** on whatever you owe.

1. **Ask your bank to lower your overdraft limit as you go.** For example, ask for £1,300 in January, £950 in April and £450 in August. This is what stops a balance from getting "stuck for two years": every time you pay it down, the room you freed up gets spent again.

# Sunday Stock Check Plan (4 hours)

**Strategy:** Count chargers first, while you're fresh, then work from highest to lowest value: screens, batteries, cases. Do the paperwork before Sunday so the 4 hours go entirely to counting.

## Before Sunday (30–60 min during the week)

- [ ] **Print or export expected stock** for every SKU from your POS or spreadsheet. Include columns for *Expected*, *Counted*, and *Difference*.
- [ ] **Pull these records for the last 3 months:**
  - Supplier deliveries and invoices (charger quantities especially)
  - Sales
  - Parts used in repairs (screens and batteries used in jobs, not sold over the counter)
  - Warranty swaps, returns, and items written off as faulty
- [ ] **Enter any unrecorded deliveries or repair jobs** so the "expected" figure is accurate. A lot of apparent loss is really paperwork.
- [ ] **Tidy storage.** Group screens by brand and model and put loose items back in their place.
- [ ] **Get supplies ready:** clipboard or tablet, pens, sticky notes or tape to mark counted shelves, and a box for "unknown/damaged" items.
- [ ] **Decide on helpers.** A second person roughly halves the time. One counts, one writes, and nobody counts an area they normally manage.

## Sunday Schedule

| Time | Task |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:15 | Lock up, turn off sales, set up sheets. No stock moves until the count is done. |
| 0:15–1:00 | **Chargers:** all locations (display, back stock, under the counter, repair bench, van/car) |
| 1:00–2:15 | **Screens:** about 30 models, roughly 2 min per model |
| 2:15–2:45 | **Batteries** |
| 2:45–3:15 | **Cases:** count by type or price band, not every design, unless they're high-value |
| 3:15–3:30 | Break, then recount anything that looked off |
| 3:30–4:00 | Compare to expected, note the gaps, list actions |

## Counting Rules

- [ ] **Count each location once, then mark it** with a sticky note so nothing is skipped or counted twice.
- [ ] **Count sealed boxes by opening a sample.** Empty or short boxes are a classic hiding spot for theft.
- [ ] **Keep separate lines for:** stock in customer repairs awaiting pickup, faulty/RMA items, and display units.
- [ ] **Recount any line that's off by more than 1–2 units** before recording it as a loss.
- [ ] **Watch for empty packaging** on shelves or in the bin. It's a strong theft signal.

## Finding the Charger Losses

For each charger SKU, calculate:

> **Opening count (3 months ago) + Received − Sold − Used/Warranty/Written off = Expected**
> **Expected − Counted = Missing**

Then look for patterns:

- **By model:** Fast or branded chargers (e.g. Apple/Samsung originals) going missing points to theft, since they're easy to resell.
- **By location:** Losses mostly from the display suggest customer theft. Losses from back stock suggest internal theft or unrecorded use.
- **By delivery:** Check whether the received count ever differed from the invoice. Suppliers sometimes short-ship.
- **By process:** Ask whether chargers get given away with repairs, lent to customers, or used on the bench without being logged.
- **By timing:** If your POS shows when stock dropped, compare that against staff rotas.

## After the Count

- [ ] Adjust stock records to the real count and note the loss value.
- [ ] **Quick fixes for chargers:**
  - Show empty boxes or dummies on display and keep the real stock behind the counter.
  - Log every charger used in a repair or given away.
  - Check deliveries against the invoice on arrival.
- [ ] **Spot-check chargers weekly** (about 10 minutes) and do a full count monthly instead of every 3 months. That way you'll know within weeks if the fixes are working.

If you share your SKU list or a POS export, I can turn this into a ready-to-print count sheet with the expected quantities filled in.

|---|---|---|

# Balcony Vegetable Garden: 2 m², Morning Sun, Low Maintenance

## What to plant

Morning sun until about 11am gives you roughly 4–5 hours of direct light. That is **partial sun**. It's good for leafy greens and herbs but not enough for crops like tomatoes, peppers, eggplant or squash, which need 6–8 hours to fruit well.

The good news is that morning sun is the gentle kind. If you're in a hot part of Brazil, your plants will be spared the harsh afternoon heat, so lettuce is less likely to bolt or turn bitter in summer.

**Best choices for your conditions:**

| Plant | Why it suits you | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cebolinha** (chives) | Very hardy, regrows after cutting | Best beginner plant |
| **Salsinha** (parsley) | Handles partial shade well | Slow to germinate; buy seedlings |
| **Couve** (collard/kale) | Productive for months, tolerates some dryness | 1 plant per large pot |
| **Rúcula** (arugula) | Fast (30–40 days), likes partial shade | Sow a little every 3–4 weeks |
| **Alface** (lettuce) | Partial sun prevents bolting | Pick heat-tolerant types (crespa, e.g. "Vanda") if it's summer where you are |
| **Hortelã** (mint) | Nearly unkillable | Always in its **own pot**, or it takes over |
| **Manjericão** (basil) | Fine with 4–5 h sun | Pinch the flowers to keep it producing |
| **Rabanete** (radish) | Ready in about 30 days | Needs pots at least 15 cm deep |

**Skip for now:** tomato, pepper, chilli, cucumber, strawberry. They'll grow but give poor harvests. If you really want to try one, cherry tomato is the most forgiving.

## Solving the watering problem

Since you can't water every day, this matters more than anything else.

1. **Self-watering pots (vasos/floreiras autoirrigáveis).** These have a water reservoir in the bottom that wicks up to the soil. Filled up, they usually last **3–5 days** for greens. This is the best use of your money.
2. **Mulch the soil surface** with dry leaves, straw or pine bark. It cuts evaporation a lot.
3. **Group your pots together.** They shade each other and hold humidity.
4. **Before each shift block,** water deeply and top up the reservoirs.
5. **Cheap backup:** a PET bottle with tiny holes in the cap, pushed upside down into the soil, gives a slow drip for 1–2 days.

## Shopping list (around R$300)

Prices are rough estimates and vary by city and store, so check locally (Cobasi, Leroy Merlin, Petz, garden centres, or Mercado Livre/Shopee).

| Item | Qty | Approx. cost |

# Balcony Vegetable Plan: 2 m × 1 m, Morning Sun Until 11am, R$300

## What your conditions allow

- **Sun:** Sun until 11am gives you about 3–5 hours of direct light. That is enough for **leafy greens and herbs** but not for fruiting crops. Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant and strawberries need 6+ hours and would give you leggy plants with little fruit, so skip them.
- **Season:** It's mid-November, heading into summer. Afternoon shade is an advantage, because it protects lettuce and arugula from the worst heat.
- **Watering:** With three 12-hour night shifts a week, you may sleep through the day after a shift. **Self-watering containers (vasos/floreiras autoirrigáveis)** are the core of this plan. Their water reservoirs keep soil moist for roughly 3–5 days in summer.
- **Space:** 2 m × 1 m means containers go along one 2 m side, leaving the rest free to walk.

## What to plant

| Container | Plants | Harvest starts |
|---|---|---|
| Floreira 1 (60 cm) | 4 lettuce seedlings, summer type: *alface crespa* (e.g., Vanda or Vera), which resists bolting in heat | ~4–5 weeks |
| Floreira 2 (60 cm) | Arugula (*rúcula*) from seed, 2 rows. Sow one row now and the second in 3 weeks for a continuous supply | ~4–5 weeks |
| Floreira 3 (60 cm) | 2 chives (*cebolinha*) + 2 parsley (*salsinha*) seedlings | Chives ~4 weeks, parsley ~6 weeks |
| Round pot (~30 cm) | 1 collard green (*couve-manteiga*) seedling | ~6–8 weeks, then leaves for many months |

All of these are cut-and-come-again crops. You pick outer leaves and the plant keeps producing, so a small space gives you steady harvests.

## Shopping list (typical 2026 prices at garden centres, Leroy Merlin, Cobasi or online)

| Item | Qty | Approx. cost |
|---|---|---|
| Self-watering planter (*floreira autoirrigável*), ~60 cm | 3 | R$120 (≈R$40 each) |
| Self-watering pot (*vaso autoirrigável*), ~30 cm diameter | 1 | R$35 |
| Vegetable potting mix (*substrato para hortaliças*), 25 L bags | 2 | R$50 |
| Worm castings (*húmus de minhoca*), 2 kg | 1 | R$15 |
| Organic fertilizer (*bokashi*), ~1 kg | 1 | R$20 |
| Pine bark mulch (*casca de pinus*), small bag | 1 | R$15 |
| Seedlings (*mudas*): 4 lettuce, 2 chives, 2 parsley, 1 collard | 9 | R$30 |
| Arugula seed packet (Isla or Feltrin) | 1 | R$5 |
| **Total** | | **≈R$290** |

That leaves about R$10 of margin. To save money, buy seedlings at a street market (*feira*), which is often cheaper than garden centres. If the planters cost more than expected, make a fourth self-watering pot from a 2 L PET bottle: cut it in half, flip the top into the bottom, and run a cotton strip through the cap as a wick.

## Setup (one afternoon)

1. **Mix the soil.** Combine both bags of substrato with the húmus. Fill containers to 2 cm below the rim.
2. **Place the containers** along the 2 m side that gets the morning sun. Put the collard pot at the end so its height doesn't shade the others. If your railing is a solid wall that shades the floor, raise the planters on bricks or a cheap stand so the plants reach the light.
3. **Plant** the seedlings at the same depth they sat in their trays. Sow arugula 0.5 cm deep in one row.
4. **Mulch** with a 2–3 cm layer of casca de pinus around the seedlings (not over the arugula seeds until they sprout). This greatly reduces evaporation.
5. **Water from the top** for the first week while roots establish, then fill the reservoirs.

## Routine that fits your shifts

- **Before each shift block:** Fill all four reservoirs to the top. This is your main watering.
- **Once on a day off:** Push a finger 3 cm into the soil. If it's dry, water from the top as well.
- **Every 3 weeks:** Sprinkle a small handful of bokashi per planter and half a handful in the collard pot.
- **Harvest** in the morning: outer leaves of lettuce, collard and parsley; arugula and chives cut 3 cm above the soil so they regrow.

This is about 10 minutes, 2–3 times a week.

## Problems to watch for

- **Lettuce bolting** (a tall central stalk and bitter leaves) during January–February heat: pull it and replace with more arugula or *almeirão*, which handle heat better.
- **Small green caterpillars or aphids on the collard:** pick them off by hand or spray diluted neutral soap (1 spoon per litre of water).
- **Wind**, if you're on a high floor: it dries containers faster. Check the reservoirs one extra time per week in the first month to learn how fast yours empty.

From about mid-December you should be harvesting arugula and lettuce, with collard and parsley following into January.

# 9-Team Barangay Basketball Tournament: Format & Schedule

**Check the dates first.** In 2026, **6 December is a Sunday and 7 December is a Monday**. The Saturday–Sunday weekend is **5–6 December**. The schedule below says "Saturday" and "Sunday", so it works for whichever dates you confirm.

## How much court time you have
- Each day runs 7:00am–5:00pm, which is 600 minutes. At 50 minutes per game, that's 12 games a day and 24 over the weekend.
- 9 teams can't all play exactly 3 games, because that would need 13.5 games. So **every team plays 4 group games**.
- That makes **18 group games, 2 semifinals and 1 final, for 21 games total.** This leaves room for a lunch break each day and some time for delays.

## Format
1. **Draw lots publicly** to give each team a number from 1 to 9.
2. **Group stage:** each team plays the 4 teams whose numbers are closest to its own, counting in a circle. For example, Team 5 plays 3, 4, 6 and 7, and Team 1 plays 8, 9, 2 and 3. Nobody plays the same team twice.
3. **Standings** are ranked by wins. If teams are tied, use these in order:
   - the result of their game against each other, if they played
   - point difference
   - fewest points allowed
   - coin toss
4. **Semifinals:** 1st vs 4th and 2nd vs 3rd. The winners play the **final on Sunday at 3:40pm**.

## Saturday: Group Stage, Day 1 (11 games)
| # | Time | Game |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7:00–7:50 | Team 1 vs Team 2 |
| 2 | 7:50–8:40 | Team 3 vs Team 4 |
| 3 | 8:40–9:30 | Team 5 vs Team 6 |
| 4 | 9:30–10:20 | Team 7 vs Team 8 |
| 5 | 10:20–11:10 | Team 2 vs Team 3 |
| 6 | 11:10–12:00 | Team 4 vs Team 5 |
| – | 12:00–12:30 | **Lunch break** |
| 7 | 12:30–1:20 | Team 6 vs Team 7 |

| 10 | 3:00–3:50 | Team 3 vs Team 5 |
| 11 | 3:50–4:40 | Team 9 vs Team 1 |

Play ends at 4:40, which leaves 20 minutes for delays.

## Sunday: Group Stage, Day 2 and Finals (10 games)

|---|---|---|
| 12 | 7:00–7:50 | Team 7 vs Team 9 |

| SF2 | 2:20–3:10 | 2nd vs 3rd |
| – | 3:10–3:40 | Rest for the finalists |
| **FINAL** | **3:40–4:30** | **Winner SF1 vs Winner SF2** |
| – | 4:30–5:00 | Awards and closing |

## What's built in
- **Every team plays 4 games**, more than your minimum of 3.
- **No team plays two games in a row.** There is always at least one game in between.
- **Each team plays 2 or 3 games on Saturday.** No team has to play 4 games in one day unless it reaches the final.
- **Finalists get at least 30 minutes of rest** before the final.

## Tips to keep it on time
- **Use short game rules.** For example, 4 quarters of 8 minutes with the clock running, stopping it only in the last 2 minutes. Long stoppages are the main reason single-court schedules fall behind.
- **Set a forfeit rule.** A team not ready 10 minutes after its start time loses by forfeit.
- **Keep a cushion on Sunday.** If things run late, shorten the lunch break rather than the finalists' rest.
- **Third-place game (optional).** To fit one in, start Sunday at 6:30am or cut the awards time.
- **Expect some fairness questions.** Teams don't all face the same opponents, so the public number draw matters. Do it openly so nobody can say the draw was rigged.
